segments.text: Have you ever read a sentence in a book that completely short-circuited your brain on the
first try?
Humans read sequentially, so when words don't align with our expectations, our comprehension
just breaks down.
Let's test that out with a famous example from linguistics.
Read this sentence on the board.
This graphic breaks down what just happened.
Looking at the first read panel on the left, that initial pass doesn't make sense.
You reach the word fell and the sentence abruptly snaps.
Did someone forget a word?
The horse raced past the barn fell?
So you read it again.
Moving to the more read section in the middle, your brain starts testing different branching
paths.
Wait, did the barn fall?
Did the horse race past the barn after the barn fell?
You test each possibility against the grammar.
Finally, looking at the right side of the diagram, the meaning clicks.
Raced isn't the main verb.
It describes the horse.
Someone raced a horse past a barn.
Then, that same horse fell.
With every repeated read, you update your understanding of the individual words, until the entire
sequence of events fits together.
And artificial intelligence doesn't read the way you do, but it untangles complex text
through a highly similar process.
It builds meaning through a sequence of repeated mathematical updates.
When you submit a prompt to an AI, the system processes your text through a massive stack
of computational filters.
That entire stack is called a neural network.
This diagram shows those filters operating.
Numbers flow in on the left.
Inside every layer, attention and transformation.
Focusing on the first block, we track starting numbers, 0.42 and negative 1.15.
Panning across the middle, these values update at each layer.
Reaching the far right, the final numbers are 0.19 and negative 1.12, proving the
data is heavily modified.
That continuous loop of attention and transformation, constantly updating the numbers at each layer,
is the machine equivalent of you rereading that confusing horse sentence.
To see exactly how that math resolves language, let's track one specific word through a new
sentence.
The tired cat sat on the mat during the May rainstorm.
It soon fell asleep.
This chart demonstrates how AI bridges those concepts.
Looking at the start panel on the left side, the word it is entirely ambiguous.
The starting numbers, 0.12 and negative 0.34, give us zero clues about what it refers to.
But moving to layer one and layer two, those numbers begin to shift.
Through the attention step, the model looks around the sentence, identifies the probable
connection between it and cat, and updates the numbers to capture that specific relationship.
Moving to the right side of the chart, this operation repeats over and over.
Every layer builds heavily on the calculations of the previous one.
By the end of the line, the final updated numbers carry the exact mathematical information
needed to firmly connect the pronoun to its subject.
Connecting it to cat is a relatively simple task, but parsing out heavy sarcasm, tracking
a complex story twist, or executing multi-step reasoning takes far more effort than our
basic examples.
To untangle those relationships, modern AI relies on enormous physical scale.
These models stack dozens and sometimes well over a hundred of these processing layers
on top of each other.
Which raises an obvious question.
If layers equal comprehension, why not just keep stacking them infinitely to create an
ever-smarter system?
The limitation is physical.
Every additional layer you stack into the network demands a massive increase in raw
computing power and processing time.
The extra benefit has to be worth the computational cost.
Meaning builds up, layer by layer.
Attention and transformation.
Dozens of times.
